newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Cause of Taiwan plane crash still unclear.
newsitem.headline: Cause of Taiwan plane crash still unclear.

text.p: Investigators on Monday failed to read the voice recorder of a domestic airliner that crashed on Taiwan's defence outpost of Matsu, killing all 16 on board, aviation officials said.
An attempted immolation of a weather observer at the Matsu airport tower raised media speculation that he gave the wrong data, but this was sternly denied by aviation authorities.

"We had difficulty making out what the pilot and co-pilot had said in the voice recorder...The noise was too loud, covering all their voice," said Chou Chih-hsiang, a section chief of the Civil Aeronautics Administration.

Chou said the administration had sent the voice recorder, recovered on Sunday near the crash site, to EVA Airways which has more high-technology devices, to try to recreate the noise-covered sound. So far no progress was reported.

The 19-seater twin-engine Formosa Airlines Dornier 228, carrying 14 passenger, a pilot and co-pilot, was on its way from the Taiwanese capital of Taipei to Matsu, which lies six miles off mainland China, when it crashed on Sunday.
Hours after the crash, a weather observer, identified as Ou-Yang Kang-yen, was found setting himself aflame, airport's police said.

Ou-Yang, who was responsible for providing weather information to the air tower officials for them to decide whether to allow a plane to land on the airport, was rushed to hospital in critical condition.
The military-controlled Matsu airport is one of the few domestic airports in Taiwan that require visual instead of computer-aided landing.

Local media speculated that Ou-Yang set himself on fire under intense guilt -- for giving the wrong information. Both the aeronautics administration and the Matsu defence command sternly denied the reports, saying despite heavy rain the weather condition at that time was still all right for landing.
